summary: This Wikipedia article describes the dry season, a yearly period of low rainfall especially in the tropics, shaped by the tropical rain belt that moves between the northern and southern tropics over the year. It covers how the rain belt timing creates dry seasons, how dry seasons cause drought and bushfires and affect grazing animals, and links dry seasons to measles spread in Africa and to foliage and ozone patterns in the Amazon.
one_line: Overview of the dry season, a yearly low-rainfall period mainly in the tropics driven by the migrating tropical rain belt.
key_facts: The dry season is a yearly period of low rainfall, especially in the tropics.
The tropical rain belt moves from the northern to the southern tropics and back over the course of the year.
The temperate counterpart to the tropical dry season is summer or winter.
The tropical rain belt lies in the southern hemisphere roughly from November to March.
From May to September, the rain belt lies in the northern hemisphere, and the southern tropics have their dry season.
Under the Köppen climate classification, a dry season month for tropical climates is one with average precipitation below 60 millimetres (2.4 in).
The rain belt reaches roughly as far north as the Tropic of Cancer and as far south as the Tropic of Capricorn.
At the equator there are two wet and two dry seasons, as the rain belt passes over twice a year.
During the dry season, humidity is very low, causing some watering holes and rivers to dry up.
Lack of water and food may force grazing animals such as zebras, elephants and giraffe to migrate to more fertile spots.
Because of the lack of water in the plants, bushfires (wildfires) are common during the dry season.
Data shows that in Africa the start of the dry season coincides with a rise in the cases of measles.
In the Amazon rainforest, foliage growth is about 25% higher with faster growth in the dry season, per the article's cited research.
Foliage growth in the Amazon appears only in the undisturbed parts of the Amazon basin, where roots can reach deeper and gather more rainwater.
Ozone levels are much higher in the dry than in the wet season in the Amazon basin, according to a 1990 study by Kirchhoff, Da Silva and Browell.
